extraction.name: Common Corpus
extraction.description: Common Corpus is the largest open dataset for language model pre-training, containing about two trillion tokens of data that are either uncopyrighted or under permissible licenses. The dataset contains a wide variety of languages, ranging from the main European languages to low-resource ones rarely present in pre-training datasets, and includes a large portion of code data. The diversity of data sources in terms of covered domains and time periods opens up paths for both research and entrepreneurial needs in diverse areas of knowledge.
extraction.license: Public Domain, CC-By, MIT, CC-By-SA, Apache-2.0, BSD-3-Clause, Open license, BSD-2-Clause, CC-BY-4.0, CC0-1.0
extraction.creator: PleIAs, Paris, France
extraction.inLanguage: Multilingual (English, French, German, Spanish, Latin, Italian, Polish, Greek, Portuguese, Russian, and many others)
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Common Corpus was assembled from multiple sources including web archives, cultural heritage institutions, government databases, scientific repositories, and code repositories. The data collection involved large-scale processing of web datasets, digitized sources, and structured data from various domains. The collection process started in May 2023 as a French corpus and expanded to become a multilingual dataset by 2024-2025.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Web API, Secondary Data analysis, Document analysis, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data comes from multiple sources: Common Crawl web archives, cultural heritage institutions (French National Library/Gallica, Library of Congress, Europeana, German Digital Library, National Library of Luxembourg, etc.), government databases (SEC, WTO, AMF, EU institutions, USPTO, UN Digital Library, OECD), scientific repositories (OpenAlex, arXiv, PubMed Central, HAL), code repositories (GitHub via The Stack v1 and v2), and Wikimedia projects (Wikipedia, Wikisource, Wikidata). Finance Commons includes 14 billion words from financial documents spanning mid-20th century to 2024. Open Culture comprises digitized monographs and periodicals from 18th-19th centuries or earlier. Open Science includes 81.1 million articles from Semantic Scholar Open Research Corpus and other scientific sources.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Data collection began in May 2023 and continued through February 2025. The temporal coverage of the collected documents varies by collection: Finance Commons spans 1993-2024 for SEC documents and 1995-2024 for WTO documents; Open Culture includes historical documents from as early as 1618 up to 1990; Legal Commons includes documents from 1658 to 2020; Open Science includes recent scientific publications; Open Code includes code from GitHub repositories.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Data manipulation included filtering by license type to retain only permissible licenses (Public Domain, CC-By, CC-By-SA, MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD variants, etc.). For Open Code, files were filtered by language and format according to file extensions, removing non-informative content like SVG files, data storage formats (csv, json), and files consisting of 75% or more digits. Manual filters were applied to discard low-quality data. Sequences of [\r]+\n were replaced with \n and line lengths were recalculated.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Preprocessing steps included: (1) Text segmentation using Segmentext model trained to handle broken and unstructured texts with digitization artifacts; (2) OCR error detection using OCRoscope (measuring non-recognized 7-grams) and OCRerrcr (DeBERTa-v2-style model with 400M parameters); (3) OCR correction using OCRonos model based on Llama 3 8B, which corrects OCR errors, wrong word cuts or merges, and broken text structures; (4) PII removal using Microsoft's Presidio with custom regular expression patterns, replacing PII with fictitious but realistic values; (5) Toxicity filtering using Celadon, a multilingual DeBERTa-v3-small classifier (~140M parameters) trained on 2M annotated samples to identify toxic content along five dimensions (race/origin bias, gender/sexuality bias, religious bias, ability bias, violence/abuse). Documents containing harmful language were either removed or synthetically rewritten.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: For toxicity detection, a multilingual toxicity classifier called Celadon was trained on 2M annotated samples. The annotations identified toxic and harmful content along five dimensions: race and origin-based bias, gender and sexuality-based bias, religious bias, ability bias, and violence and abuse.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Segmentext (text segmentation model), OCRoscope (OCR quality detection using cld2), OCRerrcr (DeBERTa-v2-style language model with 400M parameters for OCR error detection), OCRonos (Llama 3 8B-based model for OCR correction), Microsoft's Presidio (PII detection and removal), Celadon (DeBERTa-v3-small multilingual toxicity classifier with ~140M parameters), fastText (language identification)
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Common Corpus was first published in March 2024 and has undergone several releases. The current version described in this paper was released in February 2025 for the Paris AI Summit. Common Corpus will remain an evolving resource reflecting the need for a continuous open infrastructure rather than a fixed dataset, with HuggingFace ensuring proper archiving of past versions for reproducibility. The dataset is maintained by PleIAs.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Personally Identifiable Information (PII) was identified and removed using Microsoft's Presidio. PII includes phone numbers, email addresses, and IP addresses. Custom regular expression patterns were applied to increase phone number detection accuracy from 55-60% to 85%. PII was replaced with fictitious but realistic values rather than tags or removal to maintain text format and model understanding.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Common Corpus addresses legal uncertainties that have significantly impeded the development of open science research on LLMs. Previously reproducible research artifacts have been removed or taken down due to legal challenges, impacting pre-training data, models, and evaluation datasets. By providing truly open pre-training data compliant with data security regulations, Common Corpus enables LLM development while meeting legal and regulatory requirements, even in the EU where AI regulations are strictest. The dataset supports the development of fully open and auditable LLMs and serves as open science infrastructure for the entire lifecycle of language models. However, many texts in Open Culture are historical (18th-19th centuries or earlier) and do not meet modern ethical standards regarding discussion of certain ethnic groups, women, and themes such as violence.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Public Domain data in Open Culture introduces challenges as many texts are historical periodicals and monographs from at least 80 years ago. Cultural norms surrounding the discussion of certain ethnic groups, women, and themes such as violence have changed dramatically. Many of these texts do not meet modern ethical standards. Training models on these texts could lead to reproduction and circulation of harmful language. To address this, a pipeline was developed to filter public domain training data, identifying documents containing harmful language and either removing it or synthetically rewriting the document. Web data is noted as a major source of harmful and biased content, with Common Crawl shown to contain sexual content, hate speech, and racial and gender biases.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Common Corpus is far from collecting the whole range of available open data (the 'open data paradox'). The coverage for low-resource languages is still shallow. The amount of collected data (2 trillion tokens) is suitable for pre-training models of limited size but larger models will require significantly larger amounts of data. Common Corpus does not contain data for instruction-tuning or specialized tasks, so it is not directly suitable for task-specific fine-tuning. None of the curation methods could facilitate hundred-percent accuracy. OCR errors present considerable challenges to models. Some issues like OCR errors might account for better handling of typos in the future.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Common Corpus is designed for pre-training Large Language Models. It has been used to train seven European SLMs and LLMs as of May 2025, including the Pleias 1.0 family (350M, 1.2B, and 3B parameters models), Salamandra series (2B, 7B, and 40B parameters), Lucie (7B French model), and NeKo (generalist language correction model by Nvidia). Anthropic used Common Corpus in experiments for feature visualization. The dataset has also been used to create new datasets including FineVideo (43,000 YouTube videos) and Mosel (1 million audio hours). Common Corpus can be used on its own or in conjunction with existing open datasets. Use cases include Training, Testing, Validation, and Fine Tuning. The dataset is particularly useful for developing multilingual language models, historical language models, models with legal knowledge, document processing applications, coding applications, and creative writing applications.
